about.title: Napa Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Work in Napa takes many forms — vineyard rows, tasting-room floors, hotel kitchens, construction sites, and delivery routes up and down Rt 29. When a shift ends with an injury, most people assume workers' compensation is the whole story. Often it is: in California, comp is usually your exclusive remedy against your employer, and it pays regardless of who was at fault. But not every workplace injury is caused by the employer. A subcontractor who left a hazard on a job site, a property owner who ignored a broken stair, a manufacturer whose equipment failed, or another driver who hit you while you were on the clock along Soscol Avenue or Jefferson Street may all be responsible third parties, and a third-party claim is separate from comp. Napa's public record shows 253 injury collisions and 357 people injured in 2025; some of those people were working when it happened. We handle Napa workplace injury claims and can help you sort out what comp covers and whether a third-party claim exists.

items.title: Comp and third-party claims are different tracks
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the only claim you can bring against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or another driver can face a separate injury claim. We review both to understand your full picture.

items.title: The clock is already running
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and any third-party claim generally carries a 2-year deadline. Getting legal help early keeps both windows open.

items.title: Free case review, no fee unless you recover
items.desc: We provide your initial consultation at no cost, and we work on contingency. Retaliating against you for reporting an injury is illegal, and we can address that too.

items.question: I was hurt driving for work on Soscol Avenue and another driver caused it. Is that just a comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Workers' comp should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages because you were on the job, but the other driver is a third party, and California lets you bring a separate injury claim against them. That claim is where things comp doesn't pay, such as pain and suffering, can be pursued. Keep in mind the 2-year deadline applies to the third-party side.

items.question: My Napa employer says I waited too long to report. Do I still have options?
items.answer: California asks for a report within 30 days, but a late report doesn't always end the matter, especially if the employer already knew about the injury or you were getting treatment. It also has no bearing on a third-party claim against someone other than your employer. We can review the timeline and tell you where you actually stand.

items.question: Can I be fired for filing a claim after a vineyard or winery injury?
items.answer: No. Retaliating against an employee for reporting a work injury or filing for comp is illegal in California. If you are demoted, cut from the schedule, or let go after reporting, that is a separate issue worth raising with us.
